core.text: Latin's ordinary past for a finished action is **the perfect (the 'did / has done' tense)**: *pulsāvit* — he hit, or he has hit. It is built on the perfect stem (the third principal part minus -ī) with its own set of endings, used nowhere else: -ī, -istī, -it, -imus, -istis, -ērunt. Latin name: *perfectum indicātīvī āctīvī*.
English keeps two tenses apart: *I ate* (simple past) and *I have eaten* (still matters now). Latin uses one form for both; the sentence tells you which fits.
Perfect stem + -ī, -istī, -it, -imus, -istis, -ērunt. Nothing changes between stem and ending.

invented.la: Herī Iūlia rosās in hortō carpsit.
invented.en: Yesterday Julia picked roses in the garden.

core.text: Both are past, but **the imperfect (the 'was doing' tense)** paints a scene going on (*dormiēbat* — he was sleeping); the perfect reports one thing that happened (*dormīvit* — he slept). The -bā- / -ēbā- marker means imperfect; a changed stem plus -it / -ērunt means perfect.

teach.title: What the perfect does

notice.ask: Which word in each sentence says something already over and done?

teach.say: When a thing is over and done with, Latin reaches for **the perfect (the 'did / has done' tense)**: *dormīvit* — he slept, or he has slept. One Latin form covers both English pasts, and the rest of the sentence decides which to say. This is the tense stories are told in.

check.ask: Which word tells you the calling is already over?

teach.title: The stem, and the ending for 'I'
teach.say: Every perfect is built on the perfect stem: the third dictionary form with its *-ī* cut off. *lēgī* gives *lēg-*, *scrīpsī* gives *scrīps-*, *vocāvī* gives *vocāv-*. Put the *-ī* back and you have the form for 'I': *lēgī*, 'I read'. Nothing ever stands between stem and ending.

check.ask: Fill in the 'I' cell of the perfect.

teach.title: -it and -ērunt, the two a story lives on
teach.say: A story is told about other people, so these two do most of the work: *-it* for one person, *-ērunt* for more than one. *vocāvit* — he called; *lūsērunt* — they played. The *ē* of *-ērunt* is long: *lūsērunt*, never *lūserunt*.

check.ask: Fill in the two cells the story uses most.

teach.title: The three endings that carry -is-
teach.say: The rest are *-istī* for 'you', *-imus* for 'we', *-istis* for 'you all'. Two of the three carry *-is-*, which belongs to no other tense at all: *respondistī*, *mānsistis*. See *-istī* or *-istis* and the tense is settled before you even know the verb.

check.ask: Fill in the two cells that carry -is-.

teach.title: Perfect or imperfect?
teach.say: Both are past, and this is where beginners slip. **The imperfect (the 'was doing' tense)** paints a scene that is still running: *dormiēbat*, he was sleeping. The perfect reports one finished thing: *dormīvit*, he slept. Look for *-bā-* or *-ēbā-* before the ending: that is the imperfect. A changed stem with *-it* or *-ērunt* is the perfect.

check.ask: Of the two verbs here, which is the perfect, and what tells you?

teach.title: Using it
teach.say: Now say it yourself. Ørberg's usual signals for the perfect are *postquam* 'after', *iam* 'already' and *tum* 'then', and each points at something already over. The word order is free — the verb may come first — and it is still the ending, never the position, that tells you who acted.

check.ask: *taceō, tacēre, tacuī*. Put 'they fell silent' in the gap.

more.text: The learner's notes (week 21) stress that 'perfect' means completed, and that Latin's perfect doubles as the English simple past: *cibum comēdī* is 'I have eaten' or 'I ate' as the story needs.

Stem changes to know by heart: *sum → fuī*, *eō → iī* (*iit*, *iērunt*), *ferō → tulī*, *dō → dedī*, *faciō → fēcī*, *videō → vīdī*, *veniō → vēnī*. In verse and speech -ēre can replace -ērunt (*pulsāvēre*).
The *-ī* of *lēgī* and the *-ī* of *respondistī* are long too; *-it*, *-imus* and *-istis* are the short ones.
